topic.label: EEG & Signal Methods
topic.description: EEG signal processing, sleep staging, neural time series, modeling, and practical analysis methods.

papers.title: Anti-correlation time-frequency synergy and dual-granularity fusion for sleep stage classification.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep stage classification is crucial for diagnosing sleep disorders and evaluating sleep quality. Single-channel EEG sleep staging using central electrodes has garnered significant interest due to its ability to detect a higher number of sleep spindles and its cost-effectiveness. Nevertheless, several challenges remain, such as the neglect of interdependencies among features, reduced model sensitivity to the dispersion across features, potential information leakage during the learning of transition rules, and class imbalance. To address these challenges, this study specifically designs an automatic sleep staging network based on single-channel EEG. The network incorporates a multi-branch feature extraction module, which captures negatively correlated frequency features that exhibit significant variations during sleep transitions and promotes synergistic complementarity. Furthermore, a dual-granularity residual attention mechanism is employed to perform adaptive fusion along both temporal and channel dimensions based on statistical measures such as the mean and standard deviation. The causal transition-aware network ensures temporal consistency while facilitating effective learning of transition rules. The focal loss function is utilized to counteract class imbalance. Experiments on SleepEDF-20, SleepEDF-78 and SHHS datasets show that our method achieves the best performance with overall accuracy of 87.0%, 83.4% and 84.5%, respectively. For N1 stage classification which is more challenging, it reaches an accuracy of 57.5%, 52.5% and 49.3% on three datasets, respectively. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and its certain advantages over existing methods.

ai.reason: Directly addresses automatic sleep staging with single-channel EEG, spectral feature fusion and transition-aware design relevant to lightweight transferable staging.
ai.summary: Develops a single-channel EEG sleep staging network using a multi-branch module for anti-correlated frequency features, dual-granularity residual attention fusion, causal transition-aware learning, and focal loss. It reached overall accuracies of 87.0%, 83.4%, and 84.5% on SleepEDF-20, SleepEDF-78, and SHHS, respectively, including N1 accuracies of 57.5%, 52.5%, and 49.3%.

papers.title: Thalamic stereo-EEG detects sleep stages N2 and N3 with discrimination approaching scalp EEG
papers.abstract: Sleep and epilepsy interact strongly during sleep stages N2 and N3, when synchronization of brain rhythms is increased. Sleep staging relies on scalp EEG, which is often absent or incomplete during stereo-EEG monitoring and unavailable from implanted devices, while thalamic leads are increasingly implanted for epilepsy neuromodulation. Given the role of the thalamus in spindle generation and slow oscillation dynamics, we hypothesized that thalamic channels would identify N2 and N3 (N2+N3) better than other intracranial sites. We analyzed 477 h of stereo-EEG with simultaneous scalp EEG from six adults, including 46 thalamic bipolar channels on 11 electrodes. Two classifiers were evaluated on identical channels: a random forest with hidden Markov decoding (RF + HMM) trained leave-one-participant-out, and the pretrained SleepSEEG algorithm developed without thalamic channels. The primary endpoint was discrimination of N2+N3 from other stages as classified from scalp EEG by a sleep expert. Among regions sampled in all participants, thalamic channels performed best (area under the curve [AUC] 0.94 with RF + HMM and 0.93 with SleepSEEG across whole recordings; 0.88 and 0.86 at night). With RF + HMM, thalamic channels outperformed mesial temporal and temporal neocortical channels in all six participants across whole recordings. The advantage persisted against channel-count-matched subsets and a white-matter control with both classifiers. Individual thalamic electrodes reached AUCs of 0.79-0.99 with RF + HMM (10 of 11 at least 0.89). These offline findings support thalamic N2+N3 detection and motivate real-time evaluation for sleep-targeted neuromodulation.

ai.reason: Highly relevant sleep-staging study comparing transferable classifiers across recording systems (thalamic sEEG vs scalp), informs normalization and generalization.
ai.summary: Analyzed 477 h of simultaneous stereo-EEG and scalp EEG from six adults to test whether thalamic channels identify N2+N3 sleep better than other intracranial sites, using a random forest with HMM decoding and the pretrained SleepSEEG classifier. Thalamic channels performed best among regions sampled in all participants (AUC 0.94 with RF+HMM and 0.93 with SleepSEEG), supporting thalamic N2+N3 detection for sleep-targeted neuromodulation.

papers.title: EEGDash Corpus: A Training-Ready Public Corpus for EEG Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Foundation models for electroencephalography (EEG) are pretrained on tens of thousands of hours of recordings, and their accuracy grows with that amount. Such data is hard to assemble. The largest sources are clinical archives that cannot be redistributed, and the public sources are spread over several archives, file formats, and licences. We release eegdash-corpus-v0, a training-ready corpus of 77 public EEG datasets, as the gated Hugging Face dataset EEGDash/eegdash-corpus-v0 with the SHA-256 of every file. REVE, the largest published EEG foundation model, names 89 datasets as its pretraining corpus. Twelve cannot be redistributed: four clinical archives that hold 82% of its hours, and eight under no-derivatives licences. The corpus holds the 76 others that REVE's sampling rate allows and one more from REVE's release card: 77 datasets, 14,075 hours from 7,272 subjects, 5.0 million 10-second samples and 6.21 billion tokens per epoch. Every dataset is fetched through EEGDash, converted once with REVE's recipe, and stored in its own buckets of a chunked Zarr store with its licence recorded beside it, so a model can train on the whole store or on any subset of datasets. To test that the store pretrains a model, we retrain REVE-Base from scratch twice with the authors' code, changed only in how it reads data, and score it on seven public OpenEEGBench tasks. It reaches 0.331 under linear probing and 0.273 after fine-tuning, against 0.333 and 0.325 for the released model and 0.200 and 0.205 for an untrained encoder. The converter, the conversion reports, and the loader changes are released with the corpus.

ai.reason: Open, reproducible, harmonized multi-dataset EEG corpus with per-file hashes and licensing; highly valuable infrastructure for transferable, CPU-adaptable EEG methods and benchmarking.
ai.summary: Releases eegdash-corpus-v0, a training-ready corpus of 77 public EEG datasets (14,075 hours, 7,272 subjects, 5.0M 10-second samples, 6.21B tokens per epoch) packaged as a chunked Zarr store with per-file SHA-256 and licenses. Retraining REVE-Base from scratch on the corpus yields 0.331 linear-probe and 0.273 fine-tuned scores across seven OpenEEGBench tasks, versus 0.333/0.325 for the released model and 0.200/0.205 for an untrained encoder.

papers.title: Dynamics of Sleep Architecture and Nocturnal Oxygen Saturation During Acclimatization at Intermediate Altitude: A Longitudinal Observational Study in Elite Athletes.
papers.abstract: Athletes typically undergo training camps living and sleeping at intermediate altitudes (1500-2500 m). Hypoxia reshapes sleep through central circuits regulating arousal, chemoreflex gain and sympathetic outflow. However, the relationship between peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and sleep architecture and how it co-evolves during acclimatization, is unclear. We tested whether SpO2 differs across sleep stages at intermediate altitude and whether its recovery is stage specific. Seventeen mogul-ski athletes (seven women) travelled from Montréal (Canada) to Tignes (France) for a 2-week altitude training camp (AltitudeCamp; 2100 m) in June 2025. During the first week (6 nights) and the last night of AltitudeCamp, athletes were provided with a validated ring pulse oximeter and an electroencephalography (EEG) headband. We evaluated the changes in sleep stage distribution across successive nights, scored on 30-second epochs and synchronized with oximetry data. Model estimates are reported as mean ± Standard Error (SE), raw data as mean ± Standard Deviation (SD). Average total sleep time was 429 ± 47 min (mean ± SD) and did not change during AltitudeCamp (p = 0.939). Across the first week, %N3 decreased logarithmically (β = -2.35 ± 0.72%/ln (night), p = 0.002) and %Rapid eye movement sleep (REM) increased logarithmically (β = 3.13 ± 0.88%/ln (night), p < 0.001), with no changes in %Wake, %N1, or %N2. SpO2 was lower during AltitudeCamp (95.2 ± 0.3%) than measures obtained in normoxia (98 ± 0.4%; p < 0.001), and overnight heart rate (HR) was 7 ± 2 beats per minute (bpm) higher than the habitual 58 ± 3 bpm observed in normoxia (p = 0.005). Wake SpO2 increased by 0.13 ± 0.01 percentage points per night (p < 0.001), with faster recovery in N1 (0.19 ± 0.02 percentage points/night; p = 0.006) and REM (0.23 ± 0.01 percentage points/night; p < 0.001), while N2 and N3 did not differ from Wake. HR declined by 0.79 bpm/night during Wake, similar to N3 (p = 0.26), but larger than the decline in N1 (p = 0.024) and REM (p < 0.001). In N2, HR did not evolve during the first week at altitude. At intermediate altitude, nocturnal SpO2 and HR show sleep-stage-specific dynamics that mirror central ventilatory and autonomic adaptation to hypoxia. Our data suggest that acclimatization is not uniform across sleep stages, and that the first 2 nights after ascent may capture the most rapid adjustments despite similar total sleep duration. Sleep therefore offers a heterogeneous and ecologically valid index of central nervous system (CNS) acclimatization, which can be monitored longitudinally with wearable EEG-oximetry.

Over the first week %N3 decreased and %REM increased logarithmically, with sleep-stage-specific SpO2 recovery and heart-rate dynamics indicating non-uniform acclimatization across sleep stages.

papers.title: Adapting Sleep Foundation Models for Dense Sleep Spindle Localization
papers.abstract: Adapting sleep foundation models to dense electroencephalography (EEG) event localization is challenging because multi-second representations may not preserve sufficient temporal detail for precise boundary recovery. We address sleep spindle localization by adapting a frozen SleepFM encoder with a local time-frequency pathway that preserves spindle-relevant spectral content and intra-token position. The local representation drives localization, while residual cross-attention incorporates SleepFM temporal context. Dense predictions are obtained through localized token-to-sample reconstruction and temporal refinement. Tested on the Massive Online Data Annotation (MODA), the proposed model achieves an event-level $F_1$ of $0.8080 \pm 0.0040$ at IoU 0.2 across six folds. Ablations show that localization primarily depends on local spectral and sub-token temporal information, while the pretrained representation provides complementary context. These results indicate that dense adaptation benefits from preserving information below the pretrained token scale. Code will be released upon acceptance.

On MODA it achieves an event-level F1 of 0.8080 ± 0.0040 at IoU 0.2 across six folds, with ablations showing localization depends mainly on local spectral and sub-token temporal information.

papers.title: A Lightweight EEG-Based Alzheimer's Disease Detection Framework on an Edge-Computing Platform Toward Future Intelligent Digital Twin Systems.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) progresses slowly through several stages until the patient reaches full cognitive decline. The electroencephalography (EEG) alterations associated with AD often emerge before symptom onset, suggesting that accessible and repeated EEG-based assessment could facilitate earlier detection and longitudinal monitoring. However, this type of assessment requires an AD detection model operating on edge-computing platforms within the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT). At present, many existing AD detection models rely on complex deep learning architectures with numerous parameters, which significantly limit their practicality for on-edge deployment. We propose an on-edge AD detection framework comprising a lightweight dilated hybrid deep learning (DHDL) model with a channel selection approach to reduce the computational and power demands on the evaluated edge-computing platform. A key architectural component is the inclusion of dual-granularity dilated temporal convolutions. This method expands the receptive field at two scales to capture both short- and long-term temporal features from EEG signals without increasing the number of parameters. Subsequently, several hybrid lightweight layers extract distinct temporal and spatial features and are integrated with attention mechanisms. Additionally, our channel selection approach first forms an initial subset of EEG channels guided by individual channel classification accuracy, and then iteratively refines the selected channels using hill-climbing optimization. Here, we evaluated our framework on two publicly available EEG datasets recorded for the same group of subjects (n = 48 subjects): a conventional closed-eye (CE) dataset and a more challenging open-eye (OE) dataset. Validation followed a subject-independent Leave-2-Subjects-Out (L2SO) cross-validation protocol. Real-time deployment was tested on an edge-computing platform. The proposed framework achieved 92.56% accuracy for the CE dataset and 75.15% accuracy for the OE dataset. Inference required 10.45 ms and 8.23 ms per segment for the CE and OE datasets, respectively, and consumed 9.69 mJ and 6.95 mJ of energy per segment, respectively. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed framework as a real-time, on-edge inference module for AD detection. Although a complete intelligent digital twin system is not implemented in this work, the proposed framework can serve as an inference component for future digital twin systems, supporting early AD detection and progression monitoring.

ai.reason: Edge-deployable lightweight dilated CNN with channel selection matches interest in efficient, CPU/edge-friendly EEG pipelines, though clinical AD target.
ai.summary: The authors propose a lightweight dilated hybrid deep learning framework with channel selection for EEG-based Alzheimer's disease detection on edge-computing platforms. It achieved 92.56% accuracy on a closed-eye dataset and 75.15% on an open-eye dataset, with inference times of 10.45 ms and 8.23 ms per segment and energy consumption of 9.69 mJ and 6.95 mJ, respectively, demonstrating feasibility for real-time on-edge AD detection.

papers.title: Information leakage and performance overestimation in EEG-based schizophrenia detection: evidence from literature and empirical analyses.
papers.abstract: Detecting schizophrenia (SZ) from electroencephalography (EEG) signals using machine- and deep learning models gained traction lately due to potential utility in early disease detection and differential diagnosis. Classification performance reports in the range of 95% accuracy and above are common; however, review of state-of-the-art literature indicates that ~65% of published works involve erroneous practices in the evaluation pipeline such as epoch- instead of subject-based data splitting or ranking and selecting features before data partitioning. The consequent information leakage can result in an overestimation of SZ detection performance. Here we explicitly test this on three open SZ-EEG datasets using gold standard classification approaches in leaky and leakage-free implementations. Results indicate that information leakage can inflate SZ classification accuracy by up to ~30%. Accordingly, best practices regarding EEG-based SZ detection must be established and promoted before this technology can be further developed into a clinical decision-making tool.

ai.reason: Highlights data-splitting and information-leakage errors that directly affect reproducibility and evaluation of transferable EEG classifiers, useful methodological caution for sleep/vigilance pipelines.
ai.summary: Reviews EEG-based schizophrenia detection literature, finding ~65% of published works use erroneous evaluation practices (epoch-level splitting, pre-partition feature selection) that cause information leakage, and empirically tests this on three open SZ-EEG datasets with leaky versus leakage-free implementations. Information leakage inflated classification accuracy by up to ~30%, prompting calls for best-practice standards before clinical deployment.

papers.title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity
papers.abstract: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives. Randomized feature ablation inverts slope polarity in held-out trials to map the random forest models' reliance on specific rising versus falling excursions across the time-frequency space. SafeLens then establishes an empirical null by running the same pipeline on separate resting-state recordings, training forests to discriminate rest from rest. This empirical null translates each channel's complex nonlinear resting dynamics into a model-matched noise floor on the map's linear reliance scale, allowing a single threshold to control the family-wise error rate against the channel's own background structure rather than a summary statistic of its baseline. When we injected simulated cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) into resting intracranial EEG recordings, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, maintaining its advantage under trial-to-trial variability while yielding ~5-11 times fewer false components, ~2-5 times lower mean boundary error, and superior single-trial latency tracking as a timing prior. In eight patients, CCEPs remained detectable above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation, compared with 570 and 455 ms for those benchmarks. Together, these findings establish SafeLens as a novel solution for enabling nonlinear models to uncover subtle, trial-varying neural dynamics under strict statistical control.

ai.reason: Interpretable random-forest window analysis with empirical null control; a broadly useful, reproducible method for event-locked neural dynamics.
ai.summary: The authors introduce SafeLens, a nonlinear machine learning framework combining random forests with empirical null sampling to statistically control false positives when characterizing event-locked neural activity. In simulated corticocortical evoked potentials injected into intracranial EEG, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, with ~5-11 times fewer false components, and in eight patients detected CCEPs above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation versus 570 and 455 ms for benchmarks.

papers.title: Temporal Associations Between Physiological Sleep and Next-Day Pain Intensity in Individuals With Activity-Limiting Chronic Pain: A Multiple Night At-Home Ear-EEG Sleep-Monitoring Study.
papers.abstract: Chronic pain and sleep disturbances frequently co-occur. However, most prior research relies on self-report or actigraphy, which reflect behavioural aspects of sleep but provide only limited insight into the underlying sleep physiology. In this pre-registered prospective observational study (NCT06368531), we investigated within-person night-to-night variability in physiological sleep metrics and explored temporal associations between sleep metrics and next-day pain. Individuals with bothersome (n = 4) or high-impact (n = 15) chronic pain completed between 11 and 33 nights of at-home sleep monitoring using an ear-EEG device and rated morning pain intensity daily on a 0-10 numerical rating scale. This design enables assessment of real-world physiological sleep patterns alongside natural fluctuations in pain, offering a high-resolution view of sleep-pain dynamics beyond traditional diary or actigraphy-based methods. Substantial between-night variability was observed across multiple sleep metrics, such as sleep efficiency and sleep stage transitions (ICC values < 0.5), indicating that less than half of the total variance was attributable to differences between subjects, underscoring the importance of longitudinal within-person monitoring. Mixed-effects model analyses revealed that lower next-day pain intensity was associated with greater duration (β = -0.01, p = 0.005), higher percentage (β = -0.07, p = 0.001) and increased stability (β = -0.01, p = 0.013) of N3 sleep. In contrast, higher next-day pain was associated with increased N3 fragmentation (β = 0.01, p = 0.014) and a higher proportion of N1 sleep (β = 0.014, p = 0.007). Together, these findings provide objective physiological support for previously reported associations between sleep and pain, highlighting the value of longitudinal ear-EEG monitoring for capturing nightly sleep-pain dynamics. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06368531.

ai.reason: Longitudinal at-home ear-EEG sleep staging metrics and night-to-night variability; directly relevant to wearable sleep physiology and longitudinal modeling, though clinical small-N.
ai.summary: Pre-registered prospective observational study (NCT06368531) using at-home ear-EEG across 11-33 nights in 19 individuals with chronic pain to examine night-to-night sleep variability and its temporal association with next-day pain. Lower next-day pain was associated with greater N3 duration, percentage, and stability, whereas higher pain was linked to N3 fragmentation and higher N1 proportion, with ICC values below 0.5 across many sleep metrics.

papers.title: Synergistic contributions of periodic and aperiodic cortical activity to motor recovery prediction after stroke.
papers.abstract: Functional motor recovery in chronic stroke can be promoted by intensive exercise aided by neurotechnology, yet reliable physiological markers to predict recovery remain limited. Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used in clinical routines, but conventional band-power metrics conflate oscillatory (periodic) and broadband (aperiodic) activity, limiting their interpretability. Here, we tested whether EEG spectral profiles predict motor recovery in chronic stroke. Resting-state EEG (1 min) was recorded at admission and discharge using a portable system (N = 41) and parameterized with a spectral decomposition model. Parameters were examined in relation to motor improvement, as indexed by gain in a clinical score, and used to construct a prediction model. Ipsilesional periodic activity at the individual alpha frequency (IAF) significantly increased after rehabilitation (P = 0.024) and correlated with motor improvement (r = 0.39, P = 0.010). A stepwise regression model identified higher IAF peaks, steeper aperiodic slopes, and their interaction as predictors of recovery (Severe group: R 2 = 0.53, P = 0.003; balanced accuracy = 88%). The model outperformed a delta-alpha ratio-based approach commonly used in stroke prognosis. These findings indicate that the synergistic interaction between periodic and aperiodic activity provides a mechanistically meaningful and clinically relevant biomarker of residual plasticity, supporting individualized rehabilitation strategies in chronic stroke.

papers.title: Characterising cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics using TMS-EEG: The Brain Dynamic Toolbox
papers.abstract: Objective: To adapt dynamical measures used in computational and experimental perturbation models to human transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and determine whether analysis of the extended post-stimulation trajectory reveals additional features of the cortical response to long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). Methods: Single pulse and paired pulse LICI TMS-EEG responses from the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were re-analysed in 16 healthy adults. At the stimulation site, 75 single-pulse and 75 paired-pulse trials were delivered; paired pulses comprised conditioning and test stimuli separated by 100 ms. Responses from 20 frontocentral EEG channels were analysed from 50-950 ms following TMS using the open source Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox. Perturbative Integration Latency Index (PILI) indexed cortical resilience via response energy and recovery, Autocorrelation Function Width (ACFW) captured temporal memory, and Lyapunov Exponent (LE) indicated the dynamical stability. Linear mixed-effects models examined temporal, spectral, and time-frequency effects from the measured metrics. Results: LICI altered the temporal evolution of the dynamical measures. PILI distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window before converging, whereas ACFW differences persisted across a broader early interval. LE showed weaker and less consistent discrimination. Spectral effects were most evident for ACFW, while time-frequency analyses revealed later, frequency-specific LICI effects for PILI and ACFW but not LE. Conclusions: The extended post-stimulation trajectory revealed LICI-related differences in cortical resilience and temporal memory with distinct temporal and spectral profiles, while effects on dynamical stability were less consistent. Significance: The Brain Dynamic Metric Toolbox provides a reproducible framework for quantifying perturbation-recovery dynamics in TMS-EEG and demonstrates that the extended perturbational response contains information about LICI not captured by discrete early response measures.

ai.reason: Open-source dynamical-metrics toolbox (autocorrelation width, Lyapunov) aligns with dynamical-system and interpretable-tool interests, though TMS-specific.
ai.summary: The study adapted dynamical measures from computational perturbation models to TMS-EEG data and applied them to analyze cortical perturbation-recovery dynamics in 16 healthy adults during long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI). It found that LICI altered the temporal evolution of dynamical measures: Perturbative Integration Latency Index distinguished conditions in the earliest post-stimulation window, Autocorrelation Function Width differences persisted across a broader early interval, and Lyapunov Exponent showed weaker discrimination, demonstrating that extended post-stimulation trajectories reveal additional features of cortical resilience and temporal memory.

papers.title: Slow power-envelope associations among brain, heart, and gut signals during sleep: an exploratory multivariate transfer entropy study.
papers.abstract: Sleep and the brain-gut axis both involve the coordinated regulation of the central nervous system (CNS), autonomic nervous system (ANS), and enteric nervous system. Although the role of the brain-gut axis in sleep regulation is increasingly recognized, the dynamic information flow and its directionality among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep remain unclear as statistical associations. In this study, based on overnight sleep data from 24 healthy subjects, we simultaneously collected occipital electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram, and bowel sound signals, constructed a multimodal physiological signal analysis framework, and employed a multivariate transfer entropy method based on non-uniform embedding and k-nearest neighbor estimation to systematically quantify directed statistical associations at the level of slow power envelope co-modulations among the brain, heart, and gut systems within the framework of sleep staging. The results reveal a consistent pattern of directed statistical associations: information transfer from heart to brain, brain to gut, and heart to gut consistently exceeds that in the reverse directions across all sleep stages. Sleep-stage dynamics further dissociate within-system from inter-system information flow: internal information exchange within the brain and gut intensifies with sleep depth and weakens during REM, whereas inter-system pathways show divergent stage-dependent patterns: heart-to-brain flow increases from light to deep sleep, while heart-to-gut and brain-to-gut flow are suppressed during deep sleep. At the frequency-band level, the brain, heart, and gut each exhibit dynamically reorganized source-receiver roles across sleep stages, with specific frequency bands contributing differentially to each inter-system pathway depending on sleep stage. This study identifies exploratory statistical patterns of directional information flow among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep, providing hypothesis-generating observations for future studies on sleep and multi-organ interactions. These directed associations do not establish anatomical pathways, causal regulation, or clinical biomarkers, and should be regarded as exploratory.

ai.reason: Sleep-stage-linked multivariate transfer entropy analysis of multimodal signals; relevant to sleep and signal-association methods though not staging per se.
ai.summary: Using overnight EEG, ECG, and bowel sound recordings from 24 healthy subjects, the study applied multivariate transfer entropy to quantify directed slow power-envelope associations among brain, heart, and gut across sleep stages. Information flow from heart to brain, brain to gut, and heart to gut consistently exceeded reverse directions, with sleep-stage-dependent dissociation of within- versus inter-system flow, presented as exploratory statistical patterns.

papers.title: Dissociable Oscillatory Alpha and Aperiodic Neural Dynamics Underlie Atypical Attentional Control in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
papers.abstract: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often have difficulty maintaining goal-directed attention when task-relevant and task-irrelevant information compete for processing resources. The present study investigated whether this difficulty reflects distinct abnormalities in demand-related attentional regulation and distractor-related neural responses. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) signals from 45 children with ADHD and 45 typically developing (TD) children while they performed a visual detection task under low and high visual demands, with simultaneous task-irrelevant standard and deviant sounds. EEG power spectra were parameterized to separate oscillatory alpha activity from aperiodic activity, as putative indices of attentional regulation and cortical excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance, respectively. TD children showed adaptive demand-related alpha modulation, whereas children with ADHD showed an atypical alpha response pattern, including reduced frontal modulation and atypical posterior alpha enhancement; this demand-related group difference was observed in oscillatory alpha activity but not in aperiodic activity. In contrast, ADHD-related abnormalities in responses to auditory distractors were more clearly reflected in the aperiodic slope. Children with ADHD showed atypical distractor-related aperiodic modulation, suggesting reduced stability of neural background activity, potentially reflecting disrupted cortical E/I balance when irrelevant sounds had to be ignored. Furthermore, multivariate machine learning classification demonstrated that relying on these sensitive neural signatures yielded robust discrimination between children with ADHD and TD controls, with significant predictive performance emerging shortly after stimulus onset and sustaining throughout information processing. These findings suggest that oscillatory alpha activity and aperiodic neural dynamics show differential sensitivity to distinct attentional abnormalities in ADHD, with alpha oscillations primarily reflecting demand-related regulatory deficits and aperiodic activity primarily reflecting distractor-related neural instability.

papers.title: Augmented reality paradigm and EA-DGCNN decoding algorithm for motor imagery in stroke patients.
papers.abstract: Stroke represents one of the leading causes of long-term motor dysfunction on a global scale. Existing motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interface (BCI) rehabilitation training systems face critical challenges of suboptimal patient engagement and limited electroencephalography (EEG) feature decoding capacity. To overcome these challenges, this study presents two primary original contributions: an independently designed wearable augmented reality (AR) MI training paradigm and a novel Euclidean Alignment-based Dynamic Graph Convolutional Neural Network (EA-DGCNN) end-to-end decoding architecture. The immersive AR-MI paradigm heightens patient engagement and enhances MI performance. The EA-DGCNN model incorporates Euclidean alignment to minimize inter-subject variability in EEG distributions. The model extracts multi-dimensional spatiotemporal features via convolutional block attention, dynamic graph attention, and multi-scale convolutions, incorporating a Broad Learning System to achieve precise classification results. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves an accuracy of 85.13 ± 10.53% on the public BCI Competition IV 2a dataset. On a custom clinical dataset of 20 stroke patients, the AR paradigm yields a classification accuracy of 71.9 ± 8.9%, outperforming the 68.9 ± 8.0% of the traditional 2D paradigm. Furthermore, evaluations on the 64-channel PhysioNet benchmark demonstrate robust cross-subject transferability with a superior grand-average accuracy of 83.67 ± 8.52%. Neurophysiological feature analysis indicates that the AR paradigm elicits more pronounced event-related desynchronisation and event-related synchronisation responses. The t-SNE visualisation demonstrates that the AR paradigm, coupled with the proposed model, produces highly discriminative feature clustering patterns. This study delivers a more effective paradigm and a robust decoding solution for clinical BCI rehabilitation.

ai.reason: Euclidean alignment to reduce inter-subject variability and end-to-end decoding; transferable normalization/calibration idea for cross-subject EEG, though BCI-rehab specific.
ai.summary: Proposes a wearable augmented reality motor-imagery BCI training paradigm and a Euclidean Alignment-based Dynamic Graph CNN (EA-DGCNN) decoding architecture with attention, dynamic graph attention, multi-scale convolutions, and a Broad Learning System. The model reaches 85.13 ± 10.53% on BCI Competition IV 2a and 83.67 ± 8.52% cross-subject on PhysioNet, while the AR paradigm achieves 71.9 ± 8.9% versus 68.9 ± 8.0% for 2D training in 20 stroke patients.

papers.title: False-Positive Calls of Reimplemented Published Analyses for Covert Command-Following on Electroencephalograms Recorded Without Study Commands
papers.abstract: Objective: To measure how often published electroencephalographic analyses for covert command-following call patients positive without commands, and their detection of genuine responses. Methods: This cross-sectional study applied 11 reimplemented published analyses to electroencephalograms without commands: 974 clinical electroencephalography patients and, with rules fixed, 730 new patients; 38 with prolonged disorders of consciousness; and 544 comatose patients after cardiac arrest. Outcomes: false calls (share called positive) against a 5% benchmark, and genuine-response detection. Results: Three of 10 command-following analyses called significantly more than 5% of clinical electroencephalography patients positive, replicated in new patients: Goldfine 2011, a spectral test, 23.3% (95% CI, 20.2%-26.6%), above its stated 5%; du Bois 2026, a criterion for entry to brain-computer interface training, 22.2% (95% CI, 19.2%-25.5%); and Guger 2018, a P300 accuracy threshold, 13.8% (95% CI, 11.5%-16.3%), near its approximate 12% chance rate (24.5% over 2 runs). The other 7 called 0.0% to 6.9%. After cardiac arrest: 11.5% to 27.3%. All 3 detected genuine responses. Identified contributors: a variance ignoring within-command dependence (Goldfine 2011), selection over configurations and times (du Bois 2026) and a permissive threshold (Guger 2018). Goldfine 2011's command-level correction, fixed before testing, called 0.8% of new patients and 2.4% after arrest, detecting 93.4% of stroke imagery-versus-rest sessions but few between imagery types. Interpretation: Reimplemented published analyses called up to 27% of patients positive without commands, more with repeated runs. A positive result needs its complete call rule's false-call rate and detection at that rate; imagery-versus-rest detection may reflect task engagement, not imagery. The authors argue that any positive call rule must report its false-call rate and detection at that rate.

papers.title: Age-specific pediatric templates improve EEG source-reconstructed biomarkers in children
papers.abstract: EEG source reconstruction requires an anatomical head model, ideally constructed from individual magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. In developmental studies of children and adolescents, however, MRIs are rarely available. Researchers therefore routinely rely on adult templates, such as the FreeSurfer average (fsaverage), despite substantial anatomical changes throughout development. How much this reliance on adult models biases downstream EEG biomarkers remains unclear. Here, we investigated whether age-specific pediatric templates offer a better alternative to fsaverage for EEG-derived biomarkers in children and adolescents, using individual MRI-based reconstruction as the reference. We analyzed eyes-closed resting-state EEGs from 384 Healthy Brain Network participants aged 5.5 to 17.5 years. For each participant, we tested three anatomical models: their individual MRI, an age-specific pediatric template from a series spanning ages 6-17 at one-year intervals, and the adult fsaverage template. We compared four EEG biomarkers in childhood and adolescence: absolute power, relative power, long-range temporal correlations quantified with detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA), and functional excitation-inhibition (fE/I) ratio. Pediatric templates agreed more closely with individual MRI-based biomarkers in both developmental groups and had fewer parcels with significantly different biomarker values than the adult template, except for absolute power in older adolescents. We conclude that when individual MRI is not available, age-specific pediatric templates match individual MRI-based EEG biomarker values more closely than the adult template across all four biomarkers up to approximately 12 years of age and should be the preferred choice at least up to this age.

Pediatric templates matched individual MRI-based biomarker values more closely than the adult template across power, DFA, and fE/I measures up to about age 12, supporting their use when individual MRI is unavailable.

papers.title: Decoding sequence auditory expectations for clinical diagnostic and prognostic assessment of prolonged disorders of consciousness.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG) features are important objective markers for diagnostic and prognostic evaluation of prolonged disorders of consciousness (DOC). However, task-based EEG paradigms are limited by mismatches between task demands and patients' residual awareness, as well as the limited individual assessment capacity of machine-learning-based detection frameworks. In this study, we proposed a lowdemand DOC detection strategy by decoding expectations of global regularities in sequence auditory stimulation using a modified local-global paradigm. Three single-trial classification frameworks using canonical correlation analysis, principal component analysis, and xDAWN for feature extraction were developed for individualized detection of global-regularity expectations. We further established awareness evaluation criteria based on single-trial classification outcomes and evaluated their diagnostic and prognostic effectiveness in a DOC experiment. Experiments in healthy participants demonstrated that the principal components of event-related potentials associated with global regularities were preserved under the proposed detection strategy. Compared with the original local-global paradigm, this strategy significantly improved single-trial classification performance for global effects by up to 15%. Electrophysiological analyses indicated that this improvement was driven by larger EEG response differences for global effects and more stable trial-to-trial neural states. In a cohort of 20 DOC patients, the proposed evaluation criteria achieved an individual diagnostic balanced accuracy of 68.8% (sensitivity = 50%; specificity = 87.5%), and a prognostic balanced accuracy of 60.5% (sensitivity = 50%; specificity = 71%). papers.title: Feedback Valence, Prediction Error, and the Limits of Computational Attribution in Symptom-Related EEG
papers.abstract: Feedback-locked electroencephalography (EEG) responses are often interpreted using model-derived prediction errors (PEs), although signed PE can be strongly coupled to feedback valence in binary-outcome tasks. We revisited a published anxiety-related EEG association using two open probabilistic-learning datasets to examine measurement reliability, predictor separability, and participant-level recovery. In the primary dataset, greater trait anxiety was associated with a larger negative-minus-positive FCz theta response among 46 participants with elevated depressive symptoms after adjustment for depression severity. The association also differed between the sampled depression-symptom groups. The feedback contrast showed useful within-session reliability, but matched delta and P3-minus-N2 analyses did not establish theta specificity. Within participants, feedback valence and signed PE were highly correlated (r = -0.964). Exact-design simulations showed that population-level model discrimination could succeed despite poor recovery of individual neural slopes. Participant-specific learning-model refits recovered overall signed PE more consistently than the within-valence variation needed to distinguish it from feedback valence. An independent dataset reproduced the FCz feedback contrast in untreated and placebo cohorts but lacked trait-anxiety scores. Adding signed PE to valence yielded a small held-out predictive improvement under one reinforcement-learning specification, with limited support across sessions and no comparable support under the dual-rate model or in placebo. Together, these findings support a symptom-related feedback EEG association while constraining its theta-specific and participant-level computational interpretation.

Feedback valence and signed prediction error were nearly collinear (r=-0.964), and signed PE added only limited held-out predictive value beyond valence, constraining computational attribution at the individual level.

papers.title: Affective burden and resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in sleep-severity-matched chronic insomnia.
papers.abstract: Clinical heterogeneity in chronic insomnia disorder may partly reflect affective symptom burden, but its neurophysiological correlates are difficult to distinguish from those of insomnia severity. We examined whether resting-state electroencephalographic microstate dynamics differed between affective-burden phenotypes with comparable subjective sleep severity. Among 125 treatment-naive adults with chronic insomnia disorder, 21 pairs (n = 42) with low versus high affective burden, defined using prespecified Hamilton Anxiety and Depression Rating Scale thresholds, were matched 1:1 on standardized Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and Insomnia Severity Index scores. Resting-state electroencephalographic microstate features were compared between groups using linear models adjusted for residual subjective sleep severity. Further exploratory analyses of eyes-open features examined symptom associations and full-cohort dimensional associations, and evaluated classification using leave-one-pair-out cross-validation. During eyes-open rest, the high-affective-burden phenotype showed greater microstate C coverage and lower microstate D coverage, occurrence, and duration. Microstate C coverage correlated positively with a composite affective score, whereas microstate D occurrence correlated negatively with anxiety, depression, and composite affective scores. Eyes-closed analyses showed a similar trend, but the differences did not reach statistical significance. A four-feature linear support vector classifier yielded a cross-validated area under the curve of 74.8%. Corresponding effects were directionally concordant but attenuated to non-significance in full-cohort dimensional models. Although limited by the small matched sample and reliance on questionnaire-based sleep severity without objective sleep monitoring, these findings suggest that C/D microstate dynamics may be associated with affective heterogeneity in chronic insomnia. This potential association warrants further investigation in larger cohorts incorporating objective sleep measures, while the exploratory classification findings require independent external validation.

ai.summary: Matched 21 pairs of treatment-naive chronic insomnia patients on sleep severity to compare resting-state EEG microstates between low and high affective burden. High affective burden showed greater microstate C coverage and lower microstate D coverage/occurrence/duration during eyes-open rest, with a cross-validated classification AUC of 74.8%.

papers.title: Transforming neurophysiological data into measurable stress metric using machine learning-based stress quantification framework for smart factory workers.
papers.abstract: Mental stress is a common issue in demanding occupational setups, such as smart industrial settings, particularly when working with robots, being one of the primary reasons for decreased performance and productivity. Estimating and evaluating stress are critical for worker safety, performance, and overall well-being. A novel integrated framework is proposed in this research for continuous cognitive stress-level estimation that combines neuroimaging (EEG and fNIRS), gaze tracking and machine learning. A factory workers' stress assessment experiment is designed and implemented, which employs physiological, behavioral and subjective measures to assess mental stress from different perspectives. Physiological features extracted from multimodal neuroimaging data are used for training supervised classification and regression models, while gaze, behavioral, and subjective measures provide complementary evaluation of worker stress. To further optimize the pipeline, multiple feature selection algorithms are tested, followed by ensemble learning approaches, and the best model is chosen for continuous stress-level estimation. After implementing the novel stress quantification framework for the factory workers' stress assessment experiment, the ensemble learning approach produced the best results for both regression (RMSE: 10.86) and classification (accuracy: 84.1%) techniques using the STAI score as the target. The behavioral and subjective measures demonstrate the effect of varying process variables (light, noise, task speed, and complexity) during the experiment. Multimodal data, machine learning, and other computational approaches are integrated in this study to estimate continuous cognitive stress levels, utilizing the proposed framework presented in this research, thereby bridging the gap between research and practical application. The proposed multi-domain framework provides a promising solution for monitoring worker well-being in occupational settings.

ai.summary: Proposed and tested an integrated framework combining EEG, fNIRS, gaze tracking, and machine learning for continuous mental stress estimation in smart factory workers. Ensemble models using STAI scores as target achieved 84.1% classification accuracy and RMSE 10.86 for regression, with behavioral and subjective measures reflecting process-variable effects.

papers.title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging
papers.abstract: EEG extended-source imaging aims to localize active cortical regions and characterize their spatial extent, yet supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to synthetic-to-real mismatch. We propose a physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) framework for spatial source reconstruction without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining. The lead field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the INR through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. Cortical current density is modeled as a continuous coordinate-conditioned field. A classical inverse estimate provides warm initialization and spatial constraints on source activity, while patch-integrated projection maps the field to discrete source coefficients for forward modeling. Simulations with varying noise levels, source counts, and source extents showed the clearest advantage in identifying active cortical regions, particularly for multiple and larger sources. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations using real EEG recordings from epilepsy patients and intracranial stimulation experiments further supported the feasibility of the framework for source imaging. These findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised INR for extended-source imaging.

papers.title: EEG emotion-recognition datasets for neuroarchitecture: an appraisal of openness, AI-readiness and ontology maturity.
papers.abstract: Neuroarchitecture studies how designed space shapes emotion, often with electroencephalography (EEG), and computational models that decode emotion from EEG must be trained on labelled recordings. Yet none of the widely shared EEG emotion datasets was recorded while people moved through designed spaces, and the few spatial recordings we found, all released since 2023, are single studies, each cited at most once. Researchers therefore borrow general emotion datasets, recorded from seated participants watching films, listening to music, playing games or conversing, and must decide whether each can be found, obtained and reused for transfer learning. This review contributes a reusable method for that decision and applies it. Following PRISMA 2020 with the dataset as the unit of analysis, two search passes identified 27 publicly obtainable datasets (22 in the first, 5 in the second), none designed for spatial research. A published codebook of 52 criteria defines three instruments: openness, judged against the FAIR principles with access class recorded separately; AI-readiness, the equally weighted mean of three sub-scores (label information, fit to standard tasks and alignment with other data), which describes usefulness as a transfer source; and ontology maturity, on five levels, which describes how far emotion labels can be mapped onto other vocabularies. Every identifier and access route was checked. Openness was weakest in Interoperability (2.044 against a FAIR composite of 2.857), and only 8 datasets were fully open. A dataset-level identifier was missing for 13 of 27 datasets (48.1%), and three widely used datasets could not be reached through their published routes at a re-check on 11 September 2026. AI-readiness averaged 2.684 on a 1.0-4.0 scale (median 2.60, range 2.10-3.33), and ontology levels concentrated at Level 3 (16 of 27), with none at Level 4 or 5. Openness and readiness were nearly unrelated (ρ = 0.08), whereas ontology level tracked readiness (ρ = 0.68), partly because both read the label structure. Open access alone is therefore a poor guide to reuse. The method, codebook and scripts are published so that researchers in fields without dedicated data can test the datasets they plan to reuse.

Openness was weakest for Interoperability (2.044 vs FAIR composite 2.857), only 8 datasets were fully open, and ontology levels clustered at Level 3 with none at Levels 4-5.

papers.title: Generative-augmented multimodal neuroaffective decoding for product evaluation: toward neurofeedback-driven human-in-the-loop co-design.
papers.abstract: Kansei engineering traditionally relies on self-reported evaluations of product impressions, which are susceptible to contextual influences, recall bias, and assessment timing. Multimodal psychophysiological measurements offer complementary insights into affective responses, but integrating heterogeneous signals with limited sample sizes remains challenging. This study proposes Generative-Augmented Multimodal Affective Fusion (GAMAF) to predict perceived attractiveness, innovativeness, and friendliness in product evaluation. GAMAF integrates feature-space conditional Wasserstein generative adversarial learning with gradient penalty (cWGAN-GP), cross-modal attention, graph-based interactions, and adaptive modality weighting. Fifty participants evaluated three automobile cockpit designs, yielding 150 participant-stimulus trials after multimodal quality control. Electroencephalography (EEG), eye tracking (ET), and peripheral physiological signals were integrated and evaluated using nested participant-wise cross-validation. GAMAF achieved mean outer-fold R² values of 0.810, 0.850, and 0.840 for attractiveness, innovativeness, and friendliness, respectively, each with a standard deviation of 0.016. These values exceeded those of the Multimodal Transformer baseline (0.75, 0.78, and 0.76, respectively). Across the three targets, GAMAF reduced aggregate mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) by approximately 29.6% and 29.7%, respectively. Ablation analyses supported the integrated architecture, while adaptive modality weights revealed target-dependent patterns. GAMAF demonstrates the potential of generative-augmented multimodal fusion for decoding Kansei-related product impressions. However, performance comparisons remain descriptive because baseline variability and participant-level uncertainty were not quantified. Further validation on unseen product designs and closed-loop design optimization is needed to establish its generalizability and practical utility.

GAMAF reached mean outer-fold R² of 0.810, 0.850, and 0.840, exceeding a Multimodal Transformer baseline and reducing aggregate MAE and RMSE by about 29.6% and 29.7%.

papers.title: Elevated neuronal excitability and seizure susceptibility in a mouse model of SCN2A-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
papers.abstract: Pathogenic variants in SCN2A cause a spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders, including developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE). The patient-associated SCN2A-p.E430A variant selectively shifts voltage-dependence of activation, a mechanism predicted to enhance neuronal excitability. To investigate the functional consequences of the SCN2A-E430A variant, we generated the novel Scn2aE430A mouse model and assessed neuronal excitability, brain activity, seizure susceptibility, and phenytoin responsiveness. Heterozygous Scn2aE430A mice retained normal Scn2a expression levels and did not exhibit premature lethality. Hippocampal pyramidal neurons from heterozygous Scn2aE430A mice were hyperexcitable compared to wild-type neurons. Enhanced long-term potentiation was observed in the CA1 circuit of Scn2aE430A mice. Video-EEG data revealed recurrent epileptiform discharges and spectral abnormalities, but no spontaneous generalized seizure events. In multiple seizure-induction assays, Scn2aE430A mice had no difference in latency to first seizure signs, but exhibited faster seizure generalization and more lethality compared to wild-type mice, indicating alterations in seizure propagation and/or cessation rather than seizure initiation. Pretreatment with phenytoin improved seizure outcomes across all seizure induction methods. Together, these findings demonstrate that selective disruption of Scn2a activation gating is sufficient to drive neuronal hyperexcitability and network dysfunction, establishing the Scn2aE430A mouse as pharmacologically tractable model for investigating epilepsy related phenotypes associated with SCN2A gain of function.

Phenytoin pretreatment improved seizure outcomes across induction methods.

papers.title: An Eyewear-Based EEG Interface for Temporal-Region Monitoring and Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Conventional electroencephalography (EEG) devices are often impractical for ambulatory settings due to their reliance on specialized hardware and expert operation. To address this, we developed a user-friendly eyewear-based EEG system featuring dry titanium electrodes positioned approximately 5 mm inferoposterior to the T7/T8 sites (near the ears), with metal nose pads serving as references. We evaluated the system across 103 recordings spanning five paradigms: alpha reactivity, blink-related transients, fatigue, attention, and video-elicited emotion. Following quality control, 93.2-100.0% of epochs were retained. The system demonstrated high sensitivity to ocular transients, showing significant amplitude increases during the blinking task. The emotion task yielded the most robust state-related features, with statistically significant differences in differential entropy across negative, neutral, and positive video categories, achieving balanced accuracies of 0.882 for two-class and 0.667 for three-class prediction. Despite challenges at the multiple testing correction stage, the alpha reactivity and fatigue contrast tasks were still noteworthy to some extent. The attention paradigm revealed a consistent increase in differential entropy during focused states, and the eyewear system outperformed the Muse headband in group-held-out classification. These findings provide strong evidence for the feasibility of temporal-region eyewear EEG acquisition, highlighting its potential applications in the real-world, particularly for emotion recognition.

papers.title: Multiscale Neurodynamic Alterations in Major Depressive Disorder Revealed by Lempel-Ziv Complexity of Multi-Paradigm Resting-State EEG.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) abnormalities in major depressive disorder (MDD) have predominantly been examined through single-frequency band analyses or single-scale nonlinear measures, and largely within a single resting-state paradigm, which limits the characterization of regulatory interactions across temporal scales. In this study, we investigated dynamic transitions and integrative patterns of multiscale EEG activity in MDD across multiple resting-state paradigms, with a focus on characterizing alterations in multiscale neural dynamic organization. Based on multiscale Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC), we derived two classes of features quantifying the Scale-Dependent Variation Slope and the Cross-Scale Correlation Coefficient. Resting-state EEG from the MDD Patients and Healthy Controls EEG Data (MPHC) was analyzed under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions to compare multiscale regulatory dynamics between patients with MDD and healthy controls. Patients with MDD showed impaired complexity transitions from low to high frequencies and disrupted delta-centered cross-scale integration. Distinct coupling reconfiguration patterns emerged across resting states, indicating a systemic imbalance in multiscale integrative organization. Classification models built from statistically selected features performed consistently across Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbor, and Decision Tree algorithms, reaching a maximum accuracy of 85.71% with a balanced sensitivity-specificity profile. Convergent results across models further suggested the preliminary discriminative value of the proposed features within the present dataset. These findings provide a preliminary multiscale neurodynamic framework for EEG characterization in MDD and suggest that cross-scale integration differences may provide a quantitative basis for characterizing multiscale EEG dynamics in depression.

Patients showed impaired complexity transitions from low to high frequencies and disrupted delta-centered cross-scale integration, with classification reaching a maximum accuracy of 85.71%.

papers.title: EEG-based listened-language classification
papers.abstract: From an early age, individuals are continuously exposed to other languages beyond their native tongue; however, the brain s response to these auditory stimuli remains unclear. To investigate this, an experiment was designed to record electroencephalography (EEG) signals from subjects listening to sentences in five different languages, and a specific database was built to enable performing classification tests to distinguish between different languages, and varying levels of language comprehension. By analysing the energy difference between the EEG channels to characterize these signals, different classification tests were conducted using bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (bi-LSTM), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) neural networks. The main objective is the analysis of the brain s response in two different scenarios: when the subject listens to sentences in different languages, and when the subject understands or misunderstands the meaning of a sentence. In tire multi-class classification involving sentences in five different languages, the accuracy attained is 36.37 %. However, in the multi-class classification between understood/understood part of the meaning/didn t understand, the accuracy attained reaches 81.36%. The results obtained for binary classification tests of understand native language or foreign language is 89.09 %. The bi-LSTM neural network achieved the overall best performance. These results demonstrate that the analysis of the EEG signals alone can give information regarding a person s language comprehension level, and can be used for monitoring the learning curve of a new language or to assess comprehension in patients with conditions such as aphasia.

papers.title: Integrating uncertainty and practice variability for epilepsy prognostication after intracranial EEG: A meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) practices and diagnostic testing vary among institutions, limiting standardization and optimization of surgical outcomes. This study estimates resection rates and surgical outcome effect sizes after iEEG and develops individual patient-level data (IPD) models using the missing-indicator method to approximate real-world clinical uncertainties and practice variability in iEEG and surgical decision-making. Databases were queried for studies reporting ≥12-month outcomes after epilepsy surgery in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) who underwent iEEG. Random-effects meta-analysis estimated pooled outcome proportions. IPD analysis was performed using multivariable generalized linear regression and logistic regression models with cross-validation and calibration assessment. Missing values for key predictors were retained as a "not specified" category to evaluate the impact of incorporating uncertainty in common clinical data on outcome prediction. Primary outcomes were seizure freedom (Engel class IA or International League Against Epilepsy [ILAE] 1) and favorable seizure outcomes (Engel I or ILAE 1-2). Of 4975 studies identified, 115 met the inclusion criteria. The pooled frequency of patients undergoing resection after iEEG was 67% (95% confidence interval [CI] 60%-74%), 52% achieved seizure freedom (95% CI 48%-56%), and 58% achieved a favorable outcome (95% CI 54%-62%). IPD analysis included 1305 patients from 29 studies and identified a lesional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; odds ratio [OR] 1.94, CI 1.48-2.55, p < .0001) and a cortical malformation (OR 1.47, CI 1.08-2.00, p = .01) as independent predictors of a favorable outcome, whereas iEEG implantation strategy (bilateral implantation OR .61, 95% CI .42-.89, p = .01) was an independent predictor of a less favorable outcome. About two-thirds of patients undergoing iEEG proceeded to resection, and about half achieved seizure freedom. Multivariable models incorporating clinical uncertainty and practice variability were well calibrated. However, modest discrimination suggests that routinely available clinical variables alone have limited ability to predict individual surgical outcomes. More standardized and granular clinical and practice-related data may improve individualized prognostication after iEEG.

The models were well calibrated but showed only modest discrimination.

papers.title: Nociceptive-evoked electroencephalography can predict inter-individual differences in high frequency induced sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
papers.abstract: Evoked-EEG can capture changes in cortical responses during experimentally induced sensitised pain states. However, the test-retest reliability of such methods requires validation. The present study applied HFS across two identical sessions in the same individuals to assess the test-retest reliability of EEG dynamics evoked by a 128mN pin-prick stimulator and single-pulse electrical stimuli before and after HFS conditioning. The value of these features for reflecting individual differences in the development of hyperalgesia was also assessed. Results demonstrate poor-to-moderate test-retest reliability and relatively wide agreement at baseline for all features, with lateralised differences often present. This was further reduced when post-HFS changes were considered. -ERD assessed from contralateral central electrodes was significantly strengthened post-HFS for both electrical and pinprick stimuli, consistent with increased sensorimotor engagement in response to hyperalgesic and non-hyperalgesic stimuli. Notably, baseline -ERD was related to the subsequent time course of SHA development. Furthermore, whilst VP magnitude displayed a significant relationship with the general intensity of perceived pain, no specificity for SHA development was evident. Alternatively, {theta}-ERS captured a general habituation effect relative to variations in reported pain intensity between sessions for both stimuli modalities. These findings indicate that evoked EEG responses may be useful for investigating individual differences in the cortical processing of acute pain and the development time course of HFS-induced sensitivity yet may not possess sufficient test-retest reliability for interventional testing.

Reliability was poor-to-moderate and worsened for post-HFS change measures, though contralateral alpha-ERD was strengthened post-HFS and baseline alpha-ERD related to the subsequent time course of secondary hyperalgesia, while vertex potential magnitude tracked general pain intensity.

papers.title: Cannabidiol and fronto-parietal EEG connectivity in autistic children.
papers.abstract: Autistic children often show altered brain network connectivity, including circuitry implicated in social cognition. Cannabidiol (CBD) has emerged as a potential therapy for autism, but its neural mechanisms remain under-researched. Here, we analyze resting-state data collected as part of a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, to explore whether 12 weeks of oral CBD oil could modulate functional connectivity in autistic children. Twenty-nine autistic children (5 to 12 years) completed two 12-week intervention periods (CBD and placebo, randomized) separated by an 8-week washout. Before and after each period, 5 min of eyes-open resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) were obtained from a subset of 18 participants (8 female). Functional connectivity was calculated across 16 electrode-pairs in the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Beta-band connectivity between the right frontal and right inferior-parietal electrodes increased following CBD (P = 0.001, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected P [pFDR] = 0.022), and alpha connectivity showed an increase that did not remain following FDR correction (P = 0.036, pFDR = 0.428). No significant differences were observed following placebo for any frequency band (pFDR > 0.69). This study provides preliminary evidence that 12 weeks of cannabidiol is associated with an increase in right fronto-parietal (F4-P8) functional connectivity in autistic children, most pronounced in the beta-band. Replication in larger samples is needed to confirm generalizability and clinical relevance.

papers.title: Cortical evoked potentials from deep brain stimulation of the superolateral medial forebrain bundle: An exploratory study.
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation of the superolateral branch of the medial forebrain bundle (slMFB-DBS) has shown promising therapeutic effects in treatment-resistant depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Here, we explore for the first time the electrophysiological connectivity between the stimulation target and cortical sites in humans. Electrophysiological responses to single slMFB-DBS pulses were mapped in 7 patients using epidural electrocorticography (ECoG; n = 4) or high-density electroencephalography (EEG; n = 3) over 11 sessions. Electrooculography (EOG) was simultaneously recorded, given that oculomotor side-effects are common after slMFB-DBS. Cortical evoked potentials were observed in 5 of 7 patients, with consistent latencies across modalities and prefrontal EEG topographies. In one patient, screening a broad parameter space demonstrated clear modulation of ECoG responses by DBS parameters. EOG activity consistent with oculomotor nerve co-activation was present in 6 of 7 patients, yet differed in timing and morphology from cortical responses. This work shows effective connectivity between the slMFB-DBS target and the prefrontal cortex via ECoG and EEG, complementing existing structural connectivity data. This is the first exploratory study demonstrating electrophysiological connectivity between the slMFB-DBS target and the prefrontal cortex in humans, opening the door to future studies which should systematically address their robustness and suitability for objective, biomarker-guided slMFB-DBS.

papers.title: Advancing Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Depression: Novel Protocols, Precision Targeting, and Future Directions.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) remains a significant global health challenge, with substantial limitations inherent in current pharmacotherapeutic and psychotherapeutic approaches. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has emerged as a safe, effective, and non-invasive neuromodulation therapy, particularly for treatment-resistant depression (TRD). However, conventional rTMS is limited by long treatment duration and variable interindividual efficacy. This expert opinion examines recent advances in rTMS optimization strategies aimed at overcoming these limitations. Key areas of progress include the development of novel stimulation protocols such as theta-burst stimulation (TBS); accelerated regimens and priming TMS; the use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided TMS; and the integration of closed-loop systems using real-time electroencephalography (EEG) or functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) feedback. Additionally, technological innovations, including robot-assisted TMS and wearable devices, promise to enhance targeting accuracy and treatment accessibility. Despite these developments, significant challenges impede clinical translation, including the high cost of personalized protocols, insufficient standardization and validation of novel approaches, and technical barriers to closed-loop implementation. Future efforts should focus on cost reduction, large-scale randomized controlled trials, biomarker development, and device portability. Ultimately, optimized rTMS shows significant potential to become a more efficient, precise, and accessible cornerstone of depression therapy.

papers.title: A high robustness decoding technique for ultrasound modulated electroencephalogram.
papers.abstract: Ultrasound-modulated electroencephalography (USMEEG) has become a vital tool in neuroscience because it integrates millimeter-level spatial resolution with millisecond-level temporal resolution. However, under extremely complex scenarios, excessively strong or weak acoustoelectric signal coupling leads to severe distortion in USMEEG decoded signals. To address this, we developed a highly robust decoding algorithm based on the ultrasound pulse repetition frequency and introduced the acoustoelectric modulation ratio (AMR) to quantify different modulation scenarios. Across numerical simulations, phantoms, and validation using human steady-state visual evoked potential signals with data-level acoustoelectric coupling across 10 volunteers, the focused ultrasound phased array achieved an encoding spatial resolution of 0.79 millimeters. The proposed algorithm significantly outperformed four traditional methods, exhibiting higher precision under weak modulation (0 < AMR ≤ 0.6), moderate modulation (0.6 < AMR ≤ 1), and over modulation (AMR > 1) conditions, with average decoding correlations reaching 0.84, 0.90, and 0.89. This highly robust technique expands USMEEG applications and provides a technical foundation for high-performance noninvasive brain-computer interfaces.

papers.title: Yield of epileptiform abnormalities and predictors on routine electroencephalography in a neurology facility in Ghana.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is an essential neurodiagnostic tool for the evaluation of epilepsy and other neurological disorders. However, evidence on the yield of epileptiform abnormalities of routine EEG and its predictors in sub-Saharan Africa remains limited. To determine the yield of epileptiform abnormalities of routine EEG and identify factors associated with epileptiform discharges in a Ghanaian tertiary referral centre. This study included 124 patients who underwent routine outpatient EEG between October 2023 and January 2026. Demographic, clinical, medication, and EEG characteristics were collected using a standardized data extraction form. The primary outcome was the presence of epileptiform discharges. Associations between patient characteristics and epileptiform activity were assessed using Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors, with results reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The mean age of participants was 29.4 ± 19.7 years, and 55.6% were male. Epileptiform discharges were identified in 72 patients, yielding an overall epileptiform abnormality of 58.1%. Generalized epilepsy accounted for 83.3% of epileptiform abnormalities. The highest yield was observed among children aged 0-5 years (83.3%) and adults aged ≥ 60 years (75.0%). On bivariate analysis, generalized slowing (90.9%, p = 0.025) and focal slowing (100.0%, p < 0.001) were significantly associated with epileptiform discharges. In multivariable analysis, abnormal EEG background activity remained the only independent predictor of epileptiform discharges (aOR = 23.47, 95% CI: 2.95-186.86, p = 0.003). Routine EEG demonstrated a high yield of epileptiform abnormalities in this Ghanaian tertiary centre. Abnormal EEG background activity was a strong independent predictor of epileptiform discharges, highlighting the importance of careful background assessment during EEG interpretation and supporting the continued use of routine EEG in epilepsy evaluation.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Graph Analysis Reveals Enhanced Alpha-Band Integration in High-IQ Individuals: The MENSA-Connect Project.
papers.abstract: To assess whether resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) connectivity differs between high-intelligence individuals (MENSA members) and controls using graph-theory metrics: clustering coefficient, characteristic path length, and small-worldness. Resting-state 64-channel EEG data were recorded in 29 MENSA participants and 20 controls. Functional connectivity was estimated using Lagged Linear Coherence across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Graph-theory measures were computed using sLORETA and the Brain Connectivity Toolbox. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test; p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure, and effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Compared with controls, MENSA participants showed significantly lower characteristic path length in the alpha band (Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) critical value = 0.004), indicating greater global network integration. In the beta band, they showed a higher clustering coefficient (BH critical value = 0.008), reflecting greater local specialization; together with a higher characteristic path length (BH critical value = 0.013), suggesting reduced global communication. No significant group differences were observed in small-worldness across frequency bands. High-Intelligence Quotient (IQ) individuals show a frequency-dependent resting-state cortical organization, characterized by enhanced alpha-band integration and increased beta-band local specialization. These findings support a nuanced neural-efficiency model of intelligence without changes in small-world architecture. Given the cross-sectional and observational design, these findings should be regarded as associative rather than causal and require replication in larger, independent samples. These findings indicate frequency-specific differences in functional network organization, although their cognitive implications remain to be established.
