papers.title: Impairment of ictal consciousness and psychosis in drug-resistant focal epilepsy: A retrospective clinical cohort study.
papers.abstract: Psychoses of epilepsy (POE) affect up to 13% of patients with focal epilepsy. Whereas interictal risk factors are well documented, ictal correlates of POE remain poorly characterized. We hypothesized that an impairment of ictal consciousness on the Consciousness Seizure Scale (CSS), would be associated with POE. We assessed the association between ictal clinical features and POE compared to non-POE in adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. We retrospectively analyzed a presurgical cohort of adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy monitored by video-electroencephalography (EEG) or stereo-EEG. For each patient, all seizures with an examination allowing the completion of CSS score were included. POE were identified through standardized psychiatric interviews. Association between ictal features, primarily CSS score, and POE was tested using generalized estimating equations (GEE). Among 232 included seizures (25 from POE group, 207 from non-POE group), the probability of POE varied nonlinearly with ictal consciousness; it peaked at intermediate CSS scores (GEE, OR = 4.31, p = .006). This effect remained after adjustment for duration of both epilepsy (OR=1.06, p = .005) and seizure (OR=1.20, p = .013). Intraclass correlation of CSS was .76 (95%CI, .65-.85), reflecting a low within-patient variance. An older age, more severe depressive and anxiety symptoms were also associated with POE. POE were associated with intermediate impairment of ictal consciousness, suggesting that partial disruption of awareness may favor the emergence of psychotic symptoms. The high level of intrapatient stability for CSS, mostly estimated from non-POE, suggests that CSS could be constant across seizures. This raises the possibility that POE risk could stem from the way consciousness is altered during seizures.

papers.title: Matching Corticospinal and Cortical Excitability along the motor cortex: TMS-EMG-EEG study
papers.abstract: There is still no consensus on how to choose intensities for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The resting motor threshold (RMT), the intensity needed to evoke muscle contractions in the contralateral limb muscles, is a robust muscle-specific index of corticospinal excitability. RMT from one of the hand muscles is commonly used as a reference for TMS neuromodulation interventions and TMS-electroencephalography (EEG) studies. However, it only provides an indirect measure of cortical excitability, and even for the primary motor cortex (M1), we do not understand how cortical and corticospinal excitability correspond to each other. Indeed, it remains unclear whether cortical responses to TMS follow similar location-dependent patterns along the M1, and whether subthreshold stimulation can reliably engage cortical circuits relevant to motor output. Combining TMS with electromyography (EMG) and EEG, TMS-EMG-EEG, enables simultaneous assessment of corticospinal and cortical excitability to answer these questions. We investigated how cortical excitability thresholds (CETs, measured with EEG), relate to corticospinal excitability thresholds (RMTs, measured with EMG) at the hand, arm, and leg hotspots along the M1 in 24 subjects. RMTs and CETs were strongly correlated, and both increased from hand to arm to leg. CETs were generally lower than RMTs, indicating that subthreshold stimulation was enough to evoke robust early TMS evoked potentials (TEPs). Within subjects, CETs differed from the corresponding RMTs at all three M1 hotspots, and this difference increased from hand to leg representations. The findings of the present study argue against using a default hand-muscle RMT to set cortical excitability dosage along the M1 and beyond. Online TMS-EEG can enable real-time dosing and could improve stimulation precision, efficiency, and generalizability, but the site-specific variability calls for adaptive control.

papers.title: Microgravity and Cardiac Electrophysiology: Autonomic Remodeling, Arrhythmogenesis, and Implications for Long-Duration Spaceflight.
papers.abstract: In microgravity, the human heart undergoes significant geometric and functional remodeling due to the removal of gravity-dependent hydrostatic gradients. These adaptations include a transition from an elliptical to a more spherical shape configuration. Furthermore, cephalad fluid shifts trigger an early spaceflight diuresis, inducing a stable reduction in circulating plasma volume. To describe resulting electrophysiologic alterations and arrhythmia promotion. While most spaceflight arrhythmias are transient and non-lethal, they remain a concern for long-duration missions. Frequently reported irregularities include isolated premature atrial and ventricular complexes. Other events, including non-sustained ventricular tachycardia during spaceflight, the possibility of early-onset atrial fibrillation, and atherosclerosis in former astronauts following exposure to high-energy ionizing radiation have been documented, though the association is still being evaluated. The underlying arrhythmogenic substrate is driven by autonomic resetting, spatiotemporal heterogeneity, and QTc interval prolongation. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration utilizes a multi-faceted approach to maintain electrical stability, incorporating high-intensity interval training and electrolyte monitoring and supplementation. Real-time monitoring of wearable technology enables continuous telemetry of the heart. Recently, automated chest compression devices have been shown to significantly outperform manual cardiopulmonary resuscitation in microgravity environments. Although structural changes typically revert to baseline upon return to Earth gravity, deep-space missions present some risks. Astronauts exposed to ionizing radiation beyond Earth's magnetic field may face risk of long-term cardiovascular disease. Design of personalized nutrition to mitigate electrolyte loss and development of advanced screening tools for cardiac risk assessment are essential to improve the safety of future planetary missions.

papers.title: Dual-modal synaptic operation in a van der Waals heterostructure for emotion-inspired neuromorphic processing.
papers.abstract: Substantial progress has been made in artificial emotion-recognition systems; however, reproducing neurotransmitter-mediated emotional processing remains a major challenge for neuromorphic computing. In this study, we report bimodally modulated artificial synapses based on a van der Waals-stacked graphene quantum dot (GQD)/MoS2 heterostructure that integrates dopamine and optical stimuli for emotion-inspired neuromorphic processing. Incorporation of GQDs increases the ON-state current and dynamic range and improves relearning behavior and synaptic weight modulation. The GQD/MoS2 heterostructure exhibits dopamine-dependent electrical responses at concentrations of 1-5 nM and stable synaptic plasticity with retention maintained over the 1000 s measurement period. Optical stimulation in the presence of dopamine produces postsynaptic current (PSC) increases that exceed the additive expectation calculated from the individual optical-only and dopamine-only responses, supporting synergistic enhancement under the tested conditions. Device-informed facial emotion recognition simulations achieved an accuracy of 73.4% on the FER-2013 dataset using a convolutional neural network (CNN). Separately, classification of PSC-derived temporal signals using electroencephalography (EEG)-inspired processing achieved an accuracy of 76.6% with a support vector machine (SVM). These findings highlight the potential of this approach for affective computing and human-machine interaction.
